title: Heavy vs light flight on one rotation
rationale: T1 flies a light feeder cycle (DEL-JAI-DEL, 40 + 45 pax) before a full trunk cycle (DEL-BOM-DEL, 180 + 170 pax). Jaipur closes 06:30-09:30, so the feeder returns 2.5 h late and pushes the trunk flight into Mumbai's 13:00-17:00 curfew: waiting for the curfew to end would exceed the delay cap, so both trunk legs would be force-cancelled (350 pax). No spare aircraft exists: T3 is removed and T2 is already airborne on F5 (09:00) when the trunk flight needs an aircraft. Cancelling the light feeder cycle early keeps T1 at Delhi and protects the trunk rotation: 85 passengers lose their flight instead of 350. Cancelling only F1 would strand the aircraft at Delhi anyway but turn F2 into a forced cancellation, so the cycle is the clean decision.

title: Connector vs local flight
rationale: Two crews at Delhi become unavailable at 08:00 and only one standby exists, so exactly one of F3 (DEL-BOM 09:15, 60 local + 40 connecting passengers) and F5 (DEL-BOM 10:00, 90 local) can be crewed. The right call protects the connections: keep F3, and cancel the F5/F6 cycle explicitly so its passengers are re-accommodated early instead of being force-cancelled at the gate. The engine may additionally hold F3 so that F5's passengers can be moved onto it - that is a legitimate refinement, not a different decision.

title: Crew FDP breach with a standby available
rationale: A 4-hour known delay on F3 pushes crew C2 (who reported at 01:00) past their FDP. A CAT-III standby crew sits at Delhi, so the correct response is to do nothing structural: the standby takes over F3 and F4 and every flight still operates. Cancelling or delaying further would only add cost.

title: Crew FDP breach with no standby
rationale: Same delay as case 3 but the standby pool is empty. F3 cannot legally be crewed, and once it does not fly the aircraft never reaches Mumbai for F4. The clean decision is an early, explicit cancellation of the F3/F4 cycle so passengers can be re-accommodated onto F5/F6, rather than letting both become forced cancellations at the gate. A further delay on F3 is not even a candidate: it already exceeds the delay bound.

title: Curfew that no delay can recover
rationale: F3 carries a known 60-minute delay and now arrives in Mumbai at 12:15, fifteen minutes before a 12:30-14:30 curfew. It must keep moving: any further delay (the 120 and 180 minute options) would push the arrival into the curfew, and those options must be ruled out by the curfew constraint rather than scored. With F3 still flying, nothing needs to be cancelled - the right decision is to do nothing.

title: Airport capacity cut - which movement to remove
rationale: Delhi loses departure capacity from 09:00 to 14:30 (closure). F3 (09:15) would wait 5 h 15 - beyond the cancellation cap - so it cannot operate, and F4 with it; F5 (10:00) waits 4.5 h and still flies. The lowest impact decision removes the F3/F4 cycle explicitly (its passengers re-accommodate onto the delayed F5/F6) rather than letting the cascade decide. Swapping aircraft changes nothing: the constraint is the runway.

title: AOG with a spare aircraft at the hub
rationale: T1 goes technical at 08:20 after landing back in Delhi. Its remaining cycle F3/F4 (150 + 140 pax) has no aircraft, but spare T3 is parked at Delhi. Swapping the cycle onto T3 keeps every flight operating; any cancellation is strictly worse. The naive rule would cancel F4 (fewer passengers) and change nothing about F3.

title: Cancel the cycle, not the leg
rationale: Jaipur is closed from 06:30 to 12:10, so the DEL-JAI feeder F1 cannot depart within the cancellation cap. Cancelling F1 alone leaves T1 at Delhi with F2 (JAI-DEL) stranded at Jaipur as a forced cancellation; cancelling the F1/F2 cycle gives the same aircraft position with an orderly, early cancellation of both legs. Same passengers lost, no uncontrolled forced cancellation.

title: Tonight's choice vs tomorrow's first wave
rationale: A late evening cycle F7/F8 (DEL-BOM 21:00, BOM-DEL 23:30 arriving 01:30) on spare aircraft T3 is hit by a 2-hour known delay on F7. F8 would then depart Mumbai after its 00:30-06:00 curfew begins, so the cycle would strand T3 in Mumbai and leave Delhi one aircraft short for the morning wave. Cancelling the whole cycle keeps T3 in position at Delhi (next-wave shortfall 0).

title: Thin route vs trunk route - re-accommodation decides
rationale: Two crews become unavailable at Delhi and one standby remains, so one of F1 (DEL-JAI 06:00, the only Jaipur flight of the day, 100 pax) and F3 (DEL-BOM 09:15, 130 pax, with F5 DEL-BOM at 10:00 carrying 80 spare seats) must lose its crew. Cancelling the Mumbai cycle costs less because most of its passengers re-accommodate onto F5/F6 within the hour (160 of 270; 110 stranded); cancelling the Jaipur cycle strands all 200 passengers with no alternative flight. Keep the thin route, cancel the trunk cycle.

title: CAT-III qualification is the binding constraint
rationale: Delhi goes into low-visibility procedures 08:30-12:30. Crew C2 (F3/F4) is not CAT-III qualified, crews C1 and C3 are. The engine must recognise that the constraint is qualification, not duty time: the CAT-III standby S1 takes F3 and F4, nothing is cancelled, and F3 departs on time inside the fog. Doing nothing is the right decision - the standby call-out happens inside the propagation.

title: Crew-shortage day - several crews time out at once
rationale: Three rostered crews at Delhi become unavailable at 04:10 and only one standby exists. F1/F2 (C1), F3/F4 (C2) and F5/F6 (C3) all need crews; at most one cycle can be saved. The standby goes to the cycle that carries the most passengers and connections (F3/F4). The standby would otherwise be consumed by the first departure (F1), so F1/F2 must be cancelled explicitly to free it, and the F5/F6 cycle cancelled early and explicitly so their passengers are re-accommodated onto whatever still flies. The naive rule cancels by passenger count and leaves the rest to be forced at the gate.
